title: Urinalysis
summary: Urine dipstick testing and microscopy for assessment of urinary findings in fever, dysuria, and acute kidney injury.
indications: Fever in children or fever without source (UTI screening)
Acute kidney injury or renal dysfunction assessment
contraindications: None absolute, but avoid in patients with severe phimosis or urethral trauma without appropriate expertise
precautions: Use clean-catch midstream technique to minimise contamination
Label specimen immediately with patient name, date, time
Process within 30 minutes or refrigerate to prevent bacterial overgrowth
In catheterised patients, sample from catheter (not drainage bag) for culture
equipment: Sterile or clean container for specimen
preparation: Explain procedure: clean-catch midstream urine collection
Provide patient with sterile or clean container
Advise to discard initial stream and collect mid-stream
For catheterised patients: clamp catheter, allow urine to collect, sample via needle/port

steps.title: Specimen collection
steps.instruction: Patient provides clean-catch midstream urine sample (30–50 mL minimum). Ensure labelling with name, date, time immediately.
cautions: Do not contaminate specimen with patient's hands or toilet water
For catheterised patients, never sample from drainage bag
tips: Instruct patient to discard first part of stream to reduce contamination

steps.title: Visual inspection
steps.instruction: Observe colour (clear, pale, dark amber, orange, red, brown) and clarity (clear, cloudy, turbid). Record findings.
cautions: Very dark urine may indicate myoglobin or haemoglobin—note for clinical correlation
tips: Use white background to assess colour accurately
Turbidity suggests infection, crystals, or other particles

steps.title: Dipstick testing
steps.instruction: Immerse dipstick completely in urine for 1–2 seconds, withdraw and place on absorbent paper. Read results at specified times (60 seconds for most parameters, 2 minutes for nitrites/leucocyte esterase).
cautions: Do not read dipstick after 2 minutes—results become inaccurate
Store dipsticks in cool, dry place—expired or damp sticks give false results
tips: Use fresh sample—if >30 minutes old, results may be unreliable
Nitrites take 2 minutes to develop—do not read early

steps.title: Microscopy (if indicated)
steps.instruction: Centrifuge fresh urine at 400–500 g for 5 minutes. Discard supernatant, resuspend pellet in 0.5 mL urine. Place drop on slide, cover, examine under low power (x10) for casts, crystals, bacteria. Count under high power (x40) for red blood cells, white blood cells, bacteria.
cautions: Only perform if sample is fresh (<1 hour old)
Bacterial overgrowth occurs in old samples—may give false counts
tips: Use phase-contrast microscope for better visualization of casts and crystals
Count cells per low-power field (LPF) or high-power field (HPF) as appropriate

steps.title: Documentation and interpretation
steps.instruction: Record all findings (colour, clarity, dipstick results, microscopy). Correlate with clinical presentation. If UTI suspected, arrange urine culture from same specimen.
cautions: Do not report leucocyte esterase without clinical context—may indicate contamination
Asymptomatic bacteriuria requires culture confirmation; not all positive cultures indicate infection
tips: Nitrites + leucocytes + symptoms = presumed UTI; send for culture
Negative dipstick in symptomatic patient does not rule out UTI—repeat or send for culture

complications: Asymptomatic bacteriuria—common in elderly; treat only in pregnancy
False-negative dipstick—can occur if specimen >30 minutes old; consider microscopy or culture
troubleshooting: Dipstick results inconsistent with microscopy: Check specimen freshness; repeat if needed
Leucocytes on dipstick but no pyuria: May indicate contamination; repeat clean-catch specimen
Blood on dipstick with no RBCs on microscopy: May indicate myoglobin; check urine colour and clinical context
Nitrites positive but no bacteriuria: Some bacteria don't reduce nitrite; clinical context and culture matter
aftercare: Discuss results with patient if abnormalities detected
If UTI suspected: arrange culture and consider empiric antibiotic therapy if symptoms warrant
If proteinuria or haematuria: consider repeat testing, renal function assessment, and specialist referral if persistent
Document results in patient record and arrange follow-up as indicated
documentation: Record date and time of specimen collection
Document colour, clarity, and all dipstick findings
Record microscopy findings (RBCs, WBCs, bacteria, casts, crystals) if performed
Note any clinical actions taken (culture sent, antibiotics started)
escalation: Fever + pyuria (WCC >5/mL or leucocyte esterase+) + nitrites: presumed UTI—start antibiotics if symptomatic
Acute kidney injury with casts, heavy proteinuria, or haematuria: urgent hospital assessment
Haematuria without infection (RBCs without WCCs): specialist urology referral if persistent
Positive culture in pregnancy: treat to prevent pyelonephritis
competency: Able to perform clean-catch midstream urine collection technique
Familiar with correct dipstick technique and interpretation
Able to recognise normal vs abnormal urinalysis findings
Knows when to escalate (fever + pyuria, AKI signs, persistent haematuria)
